title: The List Nobody's Rating
subtitle: What the National Inventory of Dams leaves blank
voice_instructions: Measured documentary narration. Grave but restrained, never sensational. The voice of someone who has read the entire record and is quietly telling you what they found. Let the facts carry the weight; do not push. Even pacing, slight pauses at periods.
grade: Somber observational documentary still, muted desaturated color, overcast Appalachian and industrial light, cinematic wide composition, photorealistic, fine film grain, shallow depth of field, no text, no signage, no watermarks, no readable words, no identifiable faces.

beats.vo: On the morning of February 26th, 1972, a wall of black water came down a hollow in Logan County, West Virginia.
beats.img: A narrow Appalachian hollow at grey dawn, a small coal-mining community of modest houses along a creek between steep forested ridges, heavy overcast, ominous stillness before catastrophe.

beats.vo: It wasn't a river. It was coal slurry — the waste left over from washing coal — held back by a dam built out of the waste itself. The dam gave way. A hundred and twenty-five people died.
beats.cap: A coal-waste dam failed. 125 people died.
beats.img: A valley filled with black industrial sludge and debris after a flood, muddied water receding, wrecked timber, desaturated and bleak, no people, documentary aftermath, respectful and non-graphic.

beats.vo: A hundred and thirty-two million gallons of it.

card.sub: 132 million gallons of coal slurry released

beats.vo: That was fifty years ago. I wanted to know what dams like that one look like now. So I read the National Inventory of Dams — every record in it. More than ninety thousand dams.
beats.img: An endless dark government data archive rendered as towering rows of records receding into shadow, a single cold shaft of light, abstract and cinematic, sense of vast scale.

beats.vo: And I asked a simple question.

card.head: How many of the dangerous ones can the public actually look up?

beats.vo: A dam-safety inspector visits one site at a time. I can hold the whole inventory at once. And when you do that, a pattern shows up that you can't see one dam at a time.
beats.cap: One inspector, one dam at a time. I can hold all 91,678 at once.
beats.img: A lone figure in a hard hat seen from far away and from behind, standing at the foot of an enormous earthen dam, dwarfed by its scale, overcast, muted, no face visible.

beats.vo: I filtered to the dams rated high hazard — meaning if they fail, loss of human life is expected — that also have no emergency action plan on file. There are two thousand four hundred and fifty-five of them.
beats.cap: High hazard = loss of life expected if it fails.
beats.img: A large aging concrete and earthen dam holding back dark water above a small downstream town, seen from a hillside, heavy grey sky, quietly menacing, photorealistic documentary.

beats.vo: Two thousand four hundred and fifty-five dams where, if it fails, people are expected to die — and there's no plan on file for what happens then.

card.unit: high-hazard dams with no emergency action plan on file

beats.vo: Then I narrowed it to one kind in particular. The kind that failed at Buffalo Creek. Coal-slurry and mine-tailings impoundments — ponds of industrial waste, held back by earthen dams.
beats.img: Aerial view of a vast industrial tailings pond, flat grey-black waste water behind a long earthen embankment, mining infrastructure at the edges, overcast, desaturated, ominous scale.

beats.vo: Among those twenty-four hundred dams, there are thirty-seven of them.

card.sub: high hazard · no emergency action plan on file

beats.vo: And here is the part that stopped me. Twenty-one of those thirty-seven have no condition rating and no inspection date on file at all. The national database — the public's one record — goes blank exactly where the safety information should be.
beats.cap: 21 of 37: no condition rating, no inspection date on file.
beats.img: Extreme close-up of an official paper form or ledger with key fields left empty, soft focus, cold light, the blank lines emphasized, no readable text, abstract bureaucratic emptiness.

beats.vo: Twenty-one.

card.unit: with no condition rating and no inspection date on file

beats.vo: Take the tallest one. The Delbarton Slurry Impoundment, in Mingo County, West Virginia. Seven hundred and sixty feet tall — taller than any dam most Americans will ever stand under.
beats.cap: Delbarton Slurry Impoundment — Mingo County, WV
beats.img: A towering earthen impoundment dam rising hundreds of feet in a West Virginia hollow, enormous sloped wall of compacted earth, small trees for scale, low overcast light, awe and unease.

beats.vo: It holds back more than fourteen thousand acre-feet of coal slurry, above a creek called Pigeon Creek. Condition: Not Rated. Last inspection date: blank.
It's the tallest, but it isn't alone. Brushy Fork. Big Groundhog. A row of giants with the same blank fields.

It isn't only West Virginia. There's a mine-tailings dam in Polk County, Florida, last inspected in 2014. A copper-tailings dam in Arizona holding more than three hundred thousand acre-feet of waste — with no condition rating at all.
beats.cap: Florida. Arizona. Kentucky. Not just one state.
beats.img: A sun-bleached desert mine tailings impoundment in Arizona, pale dusty embankment under harsh flat light, vast and empty, industrial, desaturated, no text.

beats.vo: Now — a blank field doesn't always mean nobody is watching. Many of these are coal-mine impoundments, and coal mines answer to a different federal agency: M-S-H-A, the Mine Safety and Health Administration — not the state dam-safety programs that fill out this inventory. So some of these are inspected. Just under a different system.
beats.cap: A blank field isn't proof nobody's watching. Mines answer to MSHA, not state dam-safety.
beats.img: A weathered government regulatory office building exterior under grey sky, institutional and anonymous, muted tones, a sense of bureaucratic seams and divided responsibility.

beats.vo: But that is exactly the problem. The one place a regular person goes to look up the dam above their town — the National Inventory of Dams — can't tell you whether the biggest, most dangerous waste impoundments in the country are safe. Fifty years after Buffalo Creek, the public record still goes blank on the dams most like the one that failed.
beats.cap: The seam is the story. The public record goes blank.
beats.img: A small Appalachian town at dusk nestled directly below a steep ridge and a large earthen impoundment, warm house lights below, dark mass of the dam above, quiet tension.

beats.vo: It's a fair question to be able to answer.

card.head: Could you look up the dam above your town?

beats.vo: I can't inspect these dams. I can't tell you they're going to fail. What I can tell you is what the public record says — and what it leaves blank. That's a thing worth knowing.
beats.cap: I can't inspect them. I can tell you what the record leaves blank.
beats.img: A single small light on in a house at night in a dark Appalachian valley, the silhouette of a ridge above, quiet, intimate, documentary, muted.

beats.vo: Reading all ninety-one thousand of them took an evening. The blanks were already there. I only added them up.
You can look up the one near you.

card.head: Look up the dams near you.
